newsitem.title: DENMARK: SAS to cut Copenhagen-Stockholm fares.
newsitem.headline: SAS to cut Copenhagen-Stockholm fares.

text.p: Scandinavian Airlines System (SAS) said on Thursday that it would cut passenger fares on its Copenhagen-Stockholm route from April 1 by up to 50 percent for a limited period and up to 33 percent overall.
"There is no doubt that many of our passengers will make big savings with the new ticket types and prices," SAS director Leif Rasmussen told a news conference.
Danish airline Maersk Air last month announced that it would compete with the dominant SAS on the lucrative route from April 28, in alliance with Finland's Finnair.
SAS vowed at the time to fight back with lower fares.
It said its fully transferable business-class fare of 3,900 Danish crowns would be unaltered but a new ticket, convertible only to other SAS flights would be introduced at 2,900 crowns.

A Euro Ticket, a business class ticket to be booked at least four days ahead of travel, would cost 2,600 crowns, while an off-peak Euro-Ticket, for travel between 9.00 and 15.00 local time or after 19.00 would cost 2,400 crowns.

A standard tourist class excursion fare would fall to 2,200 crowns, Jackpot Plus --to be booked at least seven days in advance -- would be unaltered at 1,700 crowns and a Jackpot Weekend ticket would cost 1,300 crowns, SAS said.
A 40-trip season ticket in business class would fall by 47 percent to 42,000 crowns, while unlimited Copenhagen-Stockholm travel for a year could be had for 85,000, it added.

For two months from April 22, six days before the start of Maersk's service, SAS would offer two Jackpot tickets -- seven days advance booking with a Saturday night stopover condition -- for 1,500 crowns, the usual price for one.
Maersk, a unit of shipping group A.P. Moeller, said on Thursday that its cheapest fare on the route would be 1,000 crowns, available during the two months from April 28.

SAS said that the 2,900 crown Euro Express business class ticket would be reduced to 2,400 crowns during the introductory period and the off-peak version cut to 2,100 crowns, discounts of 40 percent and 33 percent off the full fare.

SAS, owned jointly by the governments of Denmark, Norway and Sweden and by private investors, said it believed that the fares and improved service -- including gateside meals -- would limit Maersk's share of traffic on the route to a maximum 20 percent.

"With the new SAS Express concept and and the many transit passengers on the route I think that Maersk Air and Finnair will have an even harder time than Braathens SAFE on the Oslo-Stockholm route," SAS director Vagn Soerensen said.
Braathens says that it got off to a bad start when it took on SAS last November, with planes carrying on average half the number of passengers needed to turn a profit.
But the Norwegian challenge hurt SAS too. Analysts estimate that prices on the route have fallen by 15 percent since Braathens started competing, costing SAS some 150 million crowns.
